html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. API: application programming interface

  • Opus, Sonnet and Haiku use cases, and the larger model above them
  • The quality, latency and cost trade-off, and routing
  • Breaking behavior changes across model releases
  • Token tracking, cost modeling and the main cost levers: caching, batch, effort, pruning

2Choosing a Model

Running case

Tidewater Picks Models

  • Three jobs: classify every incoming email (millions a month), answer adjuster questions, and investigate complex fraud cases
  • One model for everything would be either too weak or too expensive
Tier (current lineup) Strength Typical use
Haiku (for example Claude Haiku 5.5) Fastest and cheapest High-volume, latency-sensitive work: classification, routing, screening, simple extraction
Sonnet (Claude Sonnet 5.5) Best balance of speed and intelligence Most interactive applications, coding assistants, everyday agents
Opus (Claude Opus 5.5) Strong on long-running agentic and knowledge work Complex coding, multi-step agents, hard analysis; a good default when unsure
Fable (Claude Fable 5.1) Highest capability, slower and costlier The hardest reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, when Opus at high effort still falls short

  • Method: define the quality bar with evals (Module 16), try the smallest model, move up only when evals fail, and move down when a cheaper model still passes.
  • Route by difficulty (cascade): a cheap model handles the easy bulk; escalate hard or low-confidence cases to a stronger model.
  • Adaptive thinking support and effort differ by model; check the model page (Module 3).
  • "Always the largest model" and "always the smallest model" are both wrong answers: the right model is the cheapest that meets the measured requirement.

[Verify live] Current lineup and prices (per million tokens, input / output): Fable 5.1 $10 / $50, Opus 5.5 $4 / $20, Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, Haiku 5.5 from $0.10 / $0.50; all with a 1M-token context window and up to 128K output tokens. Model names, tiers and prices change; read the models overview. As of 8 November 2026.

Breaking behavior changes across releases

New models can change behavior even with the same prompt, and some parameters are removed or restricted. Examples on current models: manual extended thinking is rejected (use adaptive thinking), sampling parameters are not accepted, and forced tool use is not supported on some models.

  • Therefore: pin the model, read the migration guide before switching, re-run evals on the new model, and roll out gradually.
  • Models are retired on published dates; plan migrations early (Module 1).
Exam tip

"Upgrade to the newest model" is a release: read the migration notes, re-run evals, adjust prompts and parameters, then deploy.

Exam tip

Pick the smallest model that passes your evals; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both wrong.

3Cost and Token Management

Know what you spend

  • Track usage from the usage field of every response (input, output, cache creation and cache read tokens) and aggregate by feature, user and model. Output tokens cost more than input tokens, and thinking tokens are output tokens.
  • Estimate before sending with the token counting endpoint (an estimate) to budget, route and set limits.
  • Cost modeling: estimate tokens per request × requests per month × price, for each model; add caching and batch effects; compare options before building.

Example (illustrative): 1 million requests a month, 800 input and 150 output tokens each, on a model priced $2 input and $10 output per million: input 800M tokens = $1,600, output 150M tokens = $1,500, total about $3,100 a month; with a cached 600-token prefix read at a fraction of the input price the input cost falls sharply.

The cost levers

Lever Effect Watch out for
Smaller model / routing Lower price and latency Quality: prove with evals
Prompt caching Cache reads cost a fraction of input; faster Only stable prefixes; minimum length; TTL
Cache check-pointing (breakpoints) Cache the growing conversation prefix at chosen points Up to 4 breakpoints; order matters
Batch API 50% lower price Up to 24 h; not for waiting users
Lower effort Fewer thinking and output tokens Capability loss on hard tasks
Prune context Fewer input tokens: trim tool output, compact, drop stale history Do not drop needed facts
Limit output Concise instructions, sensible max_tokens, structured output Truncation if too low

Exam tip

Reduce cost without breaking quality: pick the lever that matches the workload (cache repeated prefixes, batch the non-urgent work, route easy cases to a small model) and verify with evals.

4Exam Q&A

S1Tidewater must label millions of incoming emails quickly and cheaply with a simple category set. Which model choice fits?

  • ANo model; guess by length
  • BThe most capable and most expensive model for every email, to be safe
  • CA small, fast model such as Haiku, checked against an eval set
  • DA random model per email
Show the answer

Answer: C. High-volume, simple, latency-sensitive tasks fit the fastest, cheapest tier once evals show the quality is sufficient.

S2A team always uses the largest model and the bill is high. Evals show a mid-tier model passes. What should they do?

  • ASwitch to the smallest model without testing
  • BKeep the largest model for safety, whatever the quality bar or the cost may be
  • CRemove the evals
  • DMove to the cheaper model that meets the quality bar, and keep monitoring
Show the answer

Answer: D. Choose the cheapest model that meets the measured requirement.

S3A system uses a cheap model for most requests and a stronger model only when confidence is low. What is this pattern?

  • AFine-tuning
  • BPrompt caching of the shared instructions
  • CBatching
  • DRouting (a cascade) by difficulty
Show the answer

Answer: D. Routing sends easy cases to a small model and escalates hard ones.

S4A developer upgrades the model name in production and answers change unexpectedly, and a parameter now returns an error. What should have been done?

  • AIncrease max_tokens
  • BRead the migration guide, re-run evals, adjust prompts, then release gradually
  • CNothing, because an upgrade never changes behavior or removes a parameter from the API
  • DDisable logging
Show the answer

Answer: B. Model changes can alter behavior and remove parameters; treat them as releases.

S5Where can a developer see how many tokens a request actually used?

  • AIn the usage field of the response
  • BIn the model's name
  • CIn the HTTP method
  • DOnly on the monthly invoice
Show the answer

Answer: A. The response usage reports input, output and cache tokens for tracking.

S6A developer wants to estimate the input size of a large prompt before sending it. What helps?

  • AThe token counting endpoint, which returns an estimate
  • BAsking the model
  • CSending the request and checking the invoice at the end of the month
  • DCounting words by hand and assuming exact equality
Show the answer

Answer: A. Token counting estimates input tokens so you can budget and route.

S7Output tokens are priced higher than input tokens. Which change is the most direct way to reduce output cost?

  • AAsk for concise answers, use structured output, and set a sensible max_tokens
  • BAdd a longer system prompt
  • CAdd more examples to the prompt
  • DIncrease the effort level
Show the answer

Answer: A. Shorter, structured output lowers the more expensive tokens.

S8An application resends the same 20,000-token policy text in every request. Which lever reduces its cost most?

  • ARemoving the policy
  • BPrompt caching of the stable prefix
  • CA higher temperature
  • DUsing batch for live chat
Show the answer

Answer: B. Cache reads of a repeated prefix cost a fraction of normal input and are faster.

S9Which TWO describe good model selection practice? Select TWO.

  • AAlways choose the largest model
  • BNever change a model once chosen
  • CRe-run evals when switching models
  • DChoose the model by its name alone
  • EDefine the quality bar with evals and choose the cheapest model that meets it
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. Evals define "good enough" and must be repeated on each model change.

S10Which TWO levers reduce cost for the nightly bulk re-tagging of old claims? Select TWO.

  • AUse fast mode for speed
  • BUse the most expensive model at maximum effort
  • CRoute easy items to a smaller model that passes the evals
  • DSubmit it as a batch for the lower price
  • EDisable the evals
Show the answer

Answer: C, D. Non-urgent bulk work suits batch pricing and routing to a cheaper model.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Tiers Haiku fastest and cheapest (volume) · Sonnet balance · Opus long agentic work (good default) · Fable hardest tasks
Method Evals set the bar; smallest model that passes; step up only when evals fail
Routing Cheap model for the bulk, escalate hard cases
Releases Pin the model; read migration notes; re-run evals; params can change
Track usage fields; token counting endpoint (estimate)
Cost Output > input price; thinking = output; cache write ~1.25x, read ~0.1x; batch −50%
Levers Smaller model · caching and breakpoints · batch · lower effort · prune context · limit output
